questions.prompt: An intervention shifts a molecular aging biomarker but does not improve tissue function. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: The biomarker changed; functional benefit remains unestablished

feedback.hint: Keep the measured endpoint separate from outcomes that were not tested.
feedback.solution: Only the measured biomarker change is established. Functional, clinical, or lifespan benefits require their own evidence and appropriate design.

questions.prompt: Why is one marker insufficient to identify senescent cells across tissues?
options: Markers can be shared with other stressed, differentiated, or lysosomal states
Every tissue has identical cell composition
A single marker proves causal function

feedback.hint: Biological states overlap in their observable features.
feedback.solution: Markers such as p16 or lysosomal activity can occur in other contexts and vary by tissue; a convergent panel and functional evidence are needed.

questions.prompt: Which result most directly supports restored stem-cell self-renewal?
options: Transient increase in a proliferation marker
Serial functional regeneration with lineage evidence and appropriate controls
Higher total DNA content in bulk tissue

feedback.hint: Self-renewal is a persistent functional property, not a snapshot count.
feedback.solution: Serial functional regeneration with lineage evidence tests sustained renewal and contribution more directly than a transient marker or bulk abundance.

questions.prompt: Why report toxicity and all randomized animals alongside functional benefit?
options: To reveal selection and competing harms that can bias an efficacy estimate
Because randomization makes missing data irrelevant

feedback.hint: Treatment-related dropout can change who remains available for analysis.
feedback.solution: If toxicity changes survival or follow-up, survivor-only analysis can be biased. Accounting for all randomized animals and harms preserves a more complete treatment comparison.
